```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

Khademioore and colleagues (2026, *Canadian Journal of Public Health*)
studied the prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) of 1.17 million singleton
births in Ontario from fiscal year 2012-2013 to 2021-2022. Among other
analyses, they fitted a joinpoint regression model to the yearly mean BMI,
selecting the number of joinpoints by BIC, and concluded that BMI was stable until 2016 and rose
afterwards. Their Table 4 reports:

| Segment | Period | Slope (95% CI) | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2012-2016 | 0.016 (-0.035, 0.067) | 0.49 |
| 2 | 2016-2021 | 0.125 (0.088, 0.162) | < 0.001 |

with a joinpoint at 2016 (95% CI 2014-2019), a slope change of 0.109 per year
(p = 0.010), and BIC values of 3.73, 2.93 and 3.33 for the models with 0, 1
and 2 joinpoints.

The article is open access (CC BY 4.0) and its appendix tabulates the yearly
data, which ship with the package as `ontario_bmi`. This vignette reproduces
the published analysis in R, draws a publication figure in place of
Figure 3, and extends the analysis to the BMI categories. Figure 4 of the
article, mean BMI by age group, ethnicity and parity, cannot be reproduced
because those yearly series are not published.

## The data

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
mb <- unique(ontario_bmi[c("year", "births", "mean_bmi", "sd_bmi")])
mb$se <- mb$sd_bmi / sqrt(mb$births)
mb
```

The standard error of each yearly mean is the standard deviation divided by
the square root of the number of births. Supplying it makes the fit
weighted by the inverse squared standard errors.

## The published model

The authors modeled mean BMI on its original scale, so the segments are
summarized by slopes in kg/m^2 per year rather than percent changes
(`log = FALSE`), and they selected the number of joinpoints by BIC with at
most two joinpoints. The article does not name its interval method; the
published intervals are symmetric around the estimates, which points to
parametric intervals.

```{r}
fit <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmax = 2,
                 method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric")
fit
```

The selection statistics, the slope change at the joinpoint and the
joinpoint itself:

```{r}
model_selection(fit)$criteria[, c("joinpoints", "sse", "bic", "selected")]
est <- model_estimates(fit)
est[est$parameter == "Slope 2 - Slope 1", c("estimate", "se", "p_value")]
joinpoints(fit)
```

The interval of the joinpoint location contains the candidate years whose
best fit with the joinpoint there has a residual sum of squares within
`Q (1 + k F / (n - p))` of the minimum `Q` (Lerman 1980), with `F` the
95% quantile of the F distribution on `k` and `n - p` degrees of freedom.
The published interval is wider. It matches the variant
`Q (1 + k / (n - p)) F`, which multiplies the whole bracket by `F` and
does not narrow as the series gets longer:

```{r}
fit_lit <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric",
                     control = jp_control(tau_interval = "literal"))
joinpoints(fit_lit)[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper")]
```

Quantity by quantity, with the package values computed from the fits
above:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
a <- apc(fit)
ci <- function(d) sprintf("(%.3f, %.3f)", d$lower, d$upper)
j <- joinpoints(fit)
jl <- joinpoints(fit_lit)
chg <- est[est$parameter == "Slope 2 - Slope 1", ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("BIC, 0 to 2 joinpoints", "Joinpoint", "Slopes",
               "Segment p values", "Slope change (p)", "Slope 95% CIs",
               "Joinpoint 95% CI"),
  Published = c("3.73, 2.93, 3.33", "2016", "0.016, 0.125", "0.49, < 0.001",
                "0.109 (0.010)", "(-0.035, 0.067), (0.088, 0.162)",
                "2014-2019"),
  Package = c(
    paste(sprintf("%.2f", model_selection(fit)$criteria$bic), collapse = ", "),
    j$estimate, paste(sprintf("%.3f", a$estimate), collapse = ", "),
    paste(ifelse(a$p_value < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.2f", a$p_value)),
          collapse = ", "),
    sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", chg$estimate, chg$p_value),
    paste(ci(a), collapse = ", "),
    sprintf("%s-%s; variant %s-%s", j$lower, j$upper, jl$lower, jl$upper)
  )
))
```

The selection, the joinpoint, the slopes, their p values and the slope
change agree with Table 4. Two quantities do not:

* The published slope limits lie inside the package's by about 0.005. They
  correspond to t quantiles on 7 to 8 degrees of freedom, while the
  published p values, like the package's slope intervals and tests, use
  the 5 degrees of freedom of the separate segment regressions. The degrees of
  freedom of the published intervals are an inference; the article does not
  report them.
* The published joinpoint interval is reproduced by the conservative
  variant only.

Because the appendix rounds the yearly means to one decimal, the remaining
digits cannot be checked further.

## A better figure

The published Figure 3 shows the yearly means and the fitted segments. The
same information, with the uncertainty of each yearly mean and the slope
intervals written on the segments, makes a cleaner figure:

```{r, fig.alt = "Mean prepregnancy BMI in Ontario by fiscal year with 95% error bars and the fitted linear joinpoint model, with the slope of each segment and its confidence interval written on the segment."}
autoplot(fit, error_bars = TRUE, labels = "ci") +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = expression("Mean BMI (kg/m"^2 * ")"))
```

`jp_table()` gives the manuscript table, including the average annual change
(AAC) over the full period, the linear model counterpart of the AAPC:

```{r}
knitr::kable(jp_table(fit, digits = 3))
```

## Extending the analysis: BMI categories

A mean can hide shifts in the tails. The appendix also gives the number of
births in each World Health Organization category, so the prevalence of each
category can be analyzed with its binomial standard error. With
`type = "percent"`, `count` and `population`, `joinpoint()` computes the
percentages and their standard errors. A log-linear model summarizes each
period by the relative change in prevalence, the natural scale for
prevalences that differ by an order of magnitude.

```{r}
fit_cat <- joinpoint(ontario_bmi, year, count = count, population = births,
                     by = "category", type = "percent", kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric")
```

On a logarithmic axis the parallel shape of the obesity classes and the
divergence of underweight and normal weight stand out:

```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Prevalence of the six BMI categories by fiscal year in one panel on a logarithmic axis, with 95% error bars and the fitted joinpoint models."}
autoplot(fit_cat, layout = "overlay", labels = "none", error_bars = TRUE,
         log_y = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence (%)")
```

Panels colored by trend direction show where each category turned:

```{r, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 8, fig.alt = "Six panels, one per BMI category, showing prevalence by fiscal year with 95% error bars, segments colored by trend direction, and the average annual percent change in each panel title."}
autoplot(fit_cat, color_by = "trend", error_bars = TRUE, aapc = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence (%)")
```

The overweight and underweight series turn in 2016, the year the mean
turned, while obesity class I was already rising from 2014. Obesity class II
rose steadily over the whole decade. The full set of trends:

```{r}
knitr::kable(jp_table(fit_cat, digits = 2))
```

## References

Khademioore S, Darling EK, D'Souza R, Muraca GM, Guo Y, Anderson LN (2026).
Prepregnancy body mass index in Ontario from 2012 to 2022: a
population-based descriptive study. *Canadian Journal of Public Health*.
doi:10.17269/s41997-026-01214-w

Lerman PM (1980). Fitting segmented regression models by grid search.
*Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C* 29:77-84.
